lines.speaker: N
lines.text: On the eighth of November, eighteen oh one, the First Consul of France told the people of Saint-Domingue, his colony in the Caribbean, that they were all French, all free and all equal.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: In the same fortnight he wrote to his foreign minister about annihilating the government of the blacks.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Five acts said free. One law said nothing. One ordinance set the price.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: The Haitian Revolution, seventeen ninety one to eighteen oh four.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Saint-Domingue, August seventeen ninety one. France's part of the island of Hispaniola, in the Caribbean, grows forty per cent of the sugar in the world, and five hundred thousand enslaved Africans grow it.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: This month the enslaved of the northern plain rise and burn the plantations. The war that follows lasts thirteen years and beats Spanish, British and French invasions.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: It ends on the first of January, eighteen oh four, when the generals of what calls itself the native army declare the colony independent and name it Haiti, the first independent Black republic.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Three accounts of how it began are held here, and disagree.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Thomas Madiou, the Haitian historian, tells of the night of the fourteenth: two hundred delegates of the workshops, the enslaved of each plantation, met at one plantation, heard a supposed decree of the king read out, and fixed the twenty second.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: The commission of the Convention, the revolutionary government in Paris, records no ceremony: the fire began towards midnight, and by the morning of the twenty third it counted thirty seven proprietors, attorneys and refiners killed.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Antoine Dalmas, a colonist writing afterwards, is the one source here for a sacrifice: a black pig, in a wooded ground called the Caiman. He dates the meeting before it, not the sacrifice.

segments.title: The night of the twenty second

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: The Cap, the colonial capital, the second of July, seventeen ninety three. France is a republic now. Polverel and Sonthonax, its two civil commissioners in the colony, print a broadside in Creole, the language of the people it addresses.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Polverel and Sonthonax, in a translation made by Void from the Creole.

lines.speaker: M
lines.text: No, this country will not die: it will never again know a king, nor know wicked masters; it will rise from its ashes, and it will be more brilliant than ever

segments.author: Etienne Polverel and Leger-Felicite Sonthonax (Void translation from the Creole)
segments.work: Proclamation of 2 July 1793, the Creole broadside, rendered by Void from the Creole

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: At the Cap, on the twenty ninth of August, Sonthonax alone proclaims for the province of the North. Article two, in a translation made by Void.

lines.speaker: M
lines.text: All the negroes and people of mixed blood now in slavery are declared free, to enjoy all the rights attached to the quality of French citizen; they will however be subject to a regime whose provisions are contained in the following articles.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: A later article binds the freed to the plantations of their former masters. Free, and bound to the same field.

segments.author: Leger-Felicite Sonthonax (Void translation from the French)
segments.work: Proclamation of 29 August 1793 for the province of the North, article II, rendered by Void from the French

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Paris, autumn eighteen oh one. Toussaint Louverture, formerly enslaved, governs the colony and has sent its constitution to Napoleon Bonaparte, First Consul, who rules France. Its twenty eighth article gives Toussaint the government for life.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: The third article of the constitution Toussaint Louverture sent, in a translation made by Void.

lines.speaker: M
lines.text: Slaves are not permitted in this territory; slavery is abolished for ever. All men born in this country live and die free men and French.

segments.author: Toussaint Louverture and the central assembly of Saint-Domingue (Void translation from the French)
segments.work: Constitution of 1801, title II, article 3, rendered by Void from the French

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: On the thirteenth of November Bonaparte wrote to Talleyrand, his foreign minister, of the course he had taken: to annihilate the government of the blacks at Saint-Domingue. His reason, in a translation made by Void.

lines.speaker: M
lines.text: I have been guided less by considerations of commerce and finance than by the necessity of stifling, in every part of the world, every kind of seed of unrest and trouble

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Talleyrand had already told the British which ships would sail: about twenty thousand men under General Leclerc, his brother-in-law.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: The next May a law maintained slavery in the colonies the peace with Britain had returned to France. It does not name Saint-Domingue.

segments.author: Napoleon Bonaparte, First Consul (Void translation from the French)
segments.work: Note to Talleyrand, 13 November 1801, rendered by Void from the French

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Saint-Domingue, June eighteen oh two. The French army has landed. Toussaint Louverture is arrested under a flag of truce, by the event record.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Toussaint Louverture, writing from the fort de Joux, his prison in the Jura mountains of France, in a translation made by Void.

lines.speaker: M
lines.text: When I was arrested, I had no other clothes than those I wore.

lines.speaker: M
lines.text: The next day my wife, together with my children who had been arrested with her, arrived there too. Sail was set at once for France.

segments.author: Toussaint Louverture (Void translation from the French)
segments.work: Memoir written at the fort de Joux, 1802, in Joseph Saint-Remy's edition of 1853, rendered by Void from the French

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: The words attributed to Toussaint Louverture aboard the ship Heros rest on one source, the memoir of Pamphile de Lacroix, a general of the expedition, in Void's translation.

lines.speaker: M
lines.text: In overthrowing me, they have cut down at Saint-Domingue only the trunk of the tree of the liberty of the blacks; it will grow back from the roots, because they are deep and many.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: On the day he died the record disagrees. Lacroix writes of cold and regret after ten months of captivity. Saint-Remy, the memoir's Haitian editor, gives the twenty seventh of April, eighteen oh three; the event record gives the seventh.

segments.author: Toussaint Louverture
segments.work: Words to Captain Savary aboard the Heros, as reported by General Pamphile de Lacroix in his memoir (1819), in Void's translation from the French

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Vertieres, outside the Cap, the eighteenth of November, eighteen oh three. The army of Jean-Jacques Dessalines, who succeeded Toussaint in command, faces the last French position. At daybreak, Madiou writes, the attack began.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: The French left within days, by the event record.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Gonaives, the army headquarters, the first of January, eighteen oh four. Dessalines, its general in chief, assembles his generals.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: The proclamation Dessalines signed that day, in the translation of Laurent Dubois and John Garrigus.

lines.speaker: M
lines.text: It is not enough to have expelled the barbarians who have bloodied our land for two centuries

lines.speaker: M
lines.text: In the end we must live independent or die.

segments.author: Jean-Jacques Dessalines
segments.work: Declaration of Independence of Haiti, in the translation of Laurent Dubois and John Garrigus

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Then the Act, which records what the generals swore before Dessalines.

lines.speaker: M
lines.text: The generals, deeply moved by these sacred principles, after voting their unanimous attachment to the declared project of independence, have all sworn to posterity, to the universe, to forever renounce France, and to die rather than to live under its domination.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: As Madiou prints it, the Act carries thirty seven names. The original, in the British National Archives, was not read here.

segments.author: Jean-Jacques Dessalines and the generals of the native army
segments.work: The Act of Independence, 1 January 1804, in the translation of Laurent Dubois and John Garrigus

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: In April Madiou prints another proclamation of Dessalines, announcing the general extermination of the French, which almost every arm, he writes, had carried out. He counts the victims, in the thousands.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Its text says its author has avenged America; the event record places those words in January, this record in April.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Five accounts of who freed whom, and what it cost.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: They are argued from what this programme could read: the acts, letters and laws of the French and Haitian states, the memoirs of a prisoner, a general and a colonist, and the abstracts of articles.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: The standard books sit in collections this programme could not open.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: The first account belongs to the people who did it. By the event record they organised through vodou, a spiritual practice forged from West African traditions under enslavement, the markets and the drums.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: None of the enslaved speaks here in his or her own words; the case is made by the state they founded.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: In May eighteen oh five Dessalines, now emperor, gave it a constitution. As Madiou prints it, in a translation made by Void.

lines.speaker: M
lines.text: The people inhabiting the island formerly called St. Domingue agree here to form themselves into a free, sovereign state, independent of all other powers of the universe, under the name of empire of Haiti.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Its second article abolishes slavery for ever. Its fourteenth says Haitians will be known only under the generic name of blacks.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Women fought at every stage, by the event record; it names Marie-Jeanne Lamartiniere. No source here is a woman's account.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: The second account is French. The event record counts its cost: roughly forty per cent of France's foreign trade, over fifty thousand men dead, and a war that yellow fever decided.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Bonaparte, to Toussaint Louverture in November eighteen oh one: Leclerc comes with forces suitable to make the sovereignty of the French people respected.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: On the fever, French scholarship has turned on itself. Bernard Gainot and Mayeul Mace, French scholars, in two thousand three.

lines.speaker: M
lines.text: The spread of yellow fever as well as the renewal of the war with Britain are facile explanations concealing the direct responsibilities of the colonial authorities.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: The third account is the Haitian state's own, from the declaration to the legislature that took on the debt. It holds that the people freed themselves and France set the price of recognising it.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: The declaration Dessalines signed puts the claim as a question, in the Dubois and Garrigus translation.

lines.speaker: M
lines.text: We have dared to be free, let us be thus by ourselves and for ourselves.

lines.speaker: M
lines.text: What people fought for us? What people wanted to gather the fruits of our labor?

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: In eighteen twenty six the Haitian legislature declared that price, a hundred and fifty million francs, a national debt, and voted a contribution over ten years to extinguish what it called a sacred engagement.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: The fourth account belongs to the scholars. The event record names its subject as silence: the scholar Michel-Rolph Trouillot's argument that the revolution was unthinkable to those who watched it, and so went unwritten.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Moses Joseph Yakubu and Paul Abiero Opondo, writing from two African universities in twenty twenty five, trace the abolition of slavery to the slave revolts, Saint-Domingue among them.

lines.speaker: M
lines.text: While the former protest was short-lived, the latter soared on to serve as an impetus for the freedom of black slaves across the globe

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: The fifth account is a receipt, and this record holds it.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Paris, the seventeenth of April, eighteen twenty five. Charles the Tenth, King of France, signs an ordinance, a royal edict.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: It requires the inhabitants of the former colony to pay a hundred and fifty million francs in five annual terms, an indemnity to compensate the former colonists, and on that condition concedes the independence, full and entire, of their government.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: It does not name the enslaved. It names the colonists. The lost property, by the event record, was five hundred thousand human beings.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: How long Haiti paid is disputed here: the one article that dates the indemnity runs it to eighteen eighty three, apart from the later loans; the event record carries the debt to nineteen forty seven.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Each is true as far as it goes.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: The account of the revolutionaries has no witness of its own here, and leaves out April eighteen oh four, which Madiou counts and defends.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: The French account leaves out the note of the thirteenth of November and the law of May eighteen oh two, the French state's papers.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: The Haitian nationalist account leaves out twenty three heads of state in the first century, most removed by force, by the event record.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: The academic account reads the record in translation, and none of its holders here counts the dead.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: The indemnity account has the ordinance and no treasury book. What was paid after eighteen twenty six is known here through two French abstracts.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: And no woman speaks here in her own words. The women appear as an arrested wife, an article of a constitution, and counted victims.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: The enslaved of Saint-Domingue rose in August seventeen ninety one. On the first of January, eighteen oh four, the generals of the native army declared the colony independent and named it Haiti.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: France recognised it in eighteen twenty five, for a hundred and fifty million francs.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Saint-Remy wrote in eighteen fifty three that Toussaint Louverture was buried as an obscure prisoner in the village cemetery below the fort, and no trace of the grave remained.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Five acts said free. One law said nothing. One ordinance set the price.
